title: The Epiphany
hook: the magi's gifts: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary, Mother of God, who kept all these words in her heart. Your line was begin with her. Did you stop and ponder before starting something? Day six hundred forty-five.

Walk down a street in parts of Poland, Germany, or a Catholic neighborhood in the American Midwest in early January, and look above the front doors. Some have letters and numbers chalked on the frame: the year, split in two, with C, M and B in between and little crosses. The letters stand for a Latin blessing, Christ bless this house, and for the three names legend gave the wise men, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. The chalk goes up on today's feast. And almost everything people think they know about those three men isn't in the Bible.
screen: `CHALK ON THE DOORFRAME.` → `C, M, B.` → `NOT IN THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Matthew calls them magoi, magi, a word for Persian priests and star-watchers. He never says there were three, and he never calls them kings. The number came later from the three gifts, the crowns from psalms about kings bringing tribute, the names from legends centuries after. What Matthew does say: they came from the east, following a star, asking, where is he that is born king of the Jews? They find the child with Mary his mother, they fall down and adore him, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "they offered him gifts; gold, frankincense, and myrrh." Early Christian writers read the gifts as a little creed. Gold, for a king. Frankincense, the incense burned in the temple, for God. Myrrh, a resin used to anoint the dead, for a man who would die. In three boxes, the whole life: royalty, divinity, and a burial. Myrrh comes back at the end of John's gospel, when Nicodemus brings a hundred pounds of it to the tomb. Epiphany comes from the Greek epiphaneia, an appearing or showing. The feast celebrates God made visible, and made visible first to outsiders: foreigners, not of Israel, who read the sky and came a long way. In the Latin West the feast centers on the magi. In many Eastern churches, the same January season celebrates the baptism in the Jordan as the great showing. It's traditionally kept on January 6, the twelfth day after Christmas, though in the United States it's moved to the nearest Sunday.
screen: `MAGI, NOT KINGS, NOT THREE.` · `THEY FELL DOWN AND ADORED.` · `KING, GOD, AND A BURIAL.` · `EPIPHANY: A SHOWING.` · then, large: `GOLD, FRANKINCENSE, AND MYRRH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a gift for someone unexpected. Not your best friend, not someone who gives to you. Someone outside your usual circle: the person who cleans your office, a neighbor you barely know, a coworker from another floor, a stranger far away. Sit and choose one person. Then choose a gift: something small, a note, a coffee, an hour of help. The magi came from outside; let your gift go outside too. If you pray, you can offer it as they did. If you don't, just plan it. The bell holds the time.
The Epiphany. From the Greek for a showing: the feast of the magi, when Christ is made known to the nations. Today's word.
Your line: gold, frankincense, myrrh. Today, give your unexpected gift, and don't explain it unless they ask. Day six hundred forty-five.

screen: `DAY 645 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BAPTISM OF THE LORD.`

howItsDone: Catholics keep the Epiphany on January 6 or, in the United States and some other countries, on the Sunday between January 2 and 8; many families have their homes blessed and chalk the doorframe that day.

original.note: Greek: magi, Persian priests and star-watchers; Matthew's word for the visitors.

trapdoor: what you thought: three kings named Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar.
what it means: magi from the east, outsiders, who adore the child and bring three gifts that tell who he is.
what a scholar hears: Matthew says magoi, no number, no crowns; gold, frankincense and myrrh were read as king, God and death by early Christian writers.
